raw_response:
*Sits down, hands folded in her lap. Speaks slowly.*

Aiya, you ask me how I'm going to farm this year? Same as last year, same as the year before. I've been doing this 45 years. My back knows the calendar better than any book — not that I could read one anyway.

Let me think out loud about my fifteen mu.

**Wheat and maize — this is my main food.** I do the wheat-maize double crop on about ten mu. That's the good flat land near the road, close to the well. My husband passed some years back, but my son comes home from town to help with the heavy jobs — the planting, the harvest. Me and my daughter-in-law handle the everyday watching and the weeding.

For the wheat I plant in October, right after the cold wind starts. I use seed I saved from last year's crop — the neighbors say use new improved seed but one bag costs money I don't have, and my saved seed has always come up fine. Before planting I put down one bag of the 复合肥 (compound) per mu — that's what the shop sells, the 15-15-15 kind, I don't know the numbers but the bag has three colors. Then when the wheat starts standing up in spring, if it looks a little yellow, I scatter half a bag of urea per mu. If the rains are good I don't need to water so much, but usually I water three times — once before winter so it doesn't freeze dry, once at jointing, once when the grain is filling. The well water costs money every time I turn on the pump, so I don't water more than I must.

For the maize, the minute the wheat is cut I have to get it in the ground — maybe four or five days, no more. My son comes with the small tractor. I don't plow deep, no time. I just scatter one bag of compound per mu and plant the hybrid seed — this one you have to buy every year, can't save it, costs about twenty yuan per mu. When it gets tall I might topdress some urea if it looks pale. Usually one or two waterings, depends on the sky.

**Cotton — three mu on the sandy piece west of the house.** My mother-in-law grew cotton, I grew cotton with her, now I still grow cotton on that sandy patch because nothing else does as well there. But it's tiring work for an old woman — the picking goes into October and my hands hurt. I only keep three mu. I buy the seed, use some compound fertilizer at planting, and I have to spray for the bollworm a few times. Cotton price isn't like before but it's still money.

**Peanut — one mu.** Peanut likes the sandy soil too. I grow it mostly for the family — we eat it, press some oil, give some to my grandchildren when they visit. Peanut doesn't need much fertilizer, my mother told me that long ago, so I just put a handful of compound and that's it. One watering maybe when it's flowering.

**Mungbean — one mu, the corner piece.** This is the lazy crop. I scatter the seed on the poor corner where nothing else grows well, don't fertilize, don't water unless there's a real drought. Maybe I get a little, maybe I get nothing. The mungbean is for soup in summer — good for the heat.

*Pauses.*

That's my year. Same plan as always. If the rain comes early I water less. If a neighbor tells me the bollworm is bad this year I buy more spray. If the fertilizer shop raises the price too much I use less urea on the topdress. That's how it goes. I don't chase big harvests — I just don't want to lose anything.
